title: Valuing a Company
blurb: P/E, EBITDA and enterprise value, discounted cash flow, startup rounds and stock options

terms.def: Net income divided by the number of shares: the profit belonging to each share.
terms.example: $10M of net income ÷ 5M shares = $2 of EPS.

terms.def: Share price divided by earnings per share: how many dollars investors pay for each $1 of yearly profit. A high P/E usually means investors expect fast growth.
terms.example: A $60 stock with $3 of EPS has a P/E of 20.

terms.def: Share price times the number of shares: what the market values the whole company's equity at.
terms.example: $50 × 20M shares = a $1B market cap.

terms.def: The yearly dividend per share divided by the price: the cash return from dividends alone.
terms.example: $2 a year on a $50 stock is a 4% dividend yield.

terms.def: A small piece of ownership in a company. Shareholders share in its profits and in changes in its value.
terms.example: Owning 100 of a company's 1,000,000 shares means owning 0.01% of it.

cards.title: Price vs profit
cards.body: A share is a slice of a company. Earnings per share tells you how much profit each slice earns. The P/E ratio compares the price with that profit: a quick way to see whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its earnings, and how much growth investors are expecting.

cards.title: Two companies
cards.body: Company A: price $40, EPS $4, so a P/E of 10. Company B: price $90, EPS $3, so a P/E of 30. B is priced for much faster growth. If B's profits stall, its price can fall hard even though the company stays profitable.

cards.title: The ratios
cards.body: EPS = net income ÷ shares. P/E = price ÷ EPS. Market cap = price × shares. Dividend yield = annual dividend ÷ price. Earnings yield, the flip side of P/E, = EPS ÷ price.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Calling a low-P/E stock automatically cheap. Sometimes the P/E is low because profits are about to fall.

checks.prompt: A stock trades at $75 and earns $5 a share. What is its P/E?
Net income is $24M and there are 8M shares. What is EPS?
A higher P/E usually means investors expect…
checks.explanation: They pay more per dollar of today's profit because they expect profits to grow.

terms.def: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: a rough measure of operating profit before financing and accounting choices.
terms.example: Operating profit of $8M + depreciation of $2M = $10M of EBITDA.

terms.def: The value of the whole business, equity plus debt minus cash: roughly what a buyer pays to own it outright.
terms.example: Market cap $80M + debt $30M − cash $10M = $100M of enterprise value.

terms.def: Debt minus cash. It is the bridge between the value of the business and the value of its shares.
terms.example: $30M of loans and $10M of cash is $20M of net debt.

terms.def: What the shareholders own: enterprise value minus net debt.
terms.example: A $100M business with $20M of net debt has $80M of equity value.
terms.formula: equity value = enterprise value − net debt

terms.def: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA. Buyers often price whole companies at a multiple of EBITDA, based on what similar companies sold for.
terms.example: A chain with $12M of EBITDA bought at 8x is valued at $96M.

terms.def: How long an investment takes to earn back what it cost.
terms.example: A $300,000 franchise earning $75,000 a year pays back in 4 years.
terms.formula: payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly cash profit

terms.def: Running a business under another company's brand and system, paying an upfront fee and usually a royalty on sales.
terms.example: A franchisee pays $50,000 upfront and 6% of sales to run a branded tea shop.

terms.def: In auctions the winner is often the bidder who most overestimated the value. Setting a walk-away price before bidding avoids overpaying.
terms.example: Bidding $120M for a business you valued at $100M just to win the deal destroys $20M of value.

cards.title: Buying the whole business
cards.body: When one company buys another, it buys the whole business, debts included. So deal makers value the business first (enterprise value), often as a multiple of EBITDA, then subtract net debt to see what the shares are worth. Discipline matters: decide your top price before the bidding starts.

cards.title: Valuing a rival chain
cards.body: The rival's EBITDA is $15M and similar chains sold for 7x. Enterprise value = $15M × 7 = $105M. It has $35M of debt and $5M of cash, so net debt is $30M. Equity value = $105M − $30M = $75M. That's the most you'd pay for the shares, before any savings from combining the two.

cards.title: The bridge
cards.body: EV = EBITDA × multiple. Net debt = debt − cash. Equity value = EV − net debt. Payback = upfront cost ÷ yearly cash profit. Franchise profit = sales − costs − royalty (royalty % × sales).

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Paying the enterprise value for the shares. If you buy the shares you also take on the debt, so it must be subtracted.

checks.prompt: EBITDA is $20M and the multiple is 6x. What is the enterprise value?
Enterprise value $120M, debt $40M, cash $10M. What is the equity value?
A $200,000 franchise earns $50,000 a year in cash. What is the payback period?

terms.def: Valuing a company as the present value of all the cash it is expected to produce in the future.
terms.example: Project five years of free cash flow, add a terminal value and discount everything back to today.

terms.def: The value of all cash flows beyond the forecast years, usually assuming steady growth forever. It is often most of a DCF's value.
terms.example: Year-5 cash of $10M growing 2% forever at a 9% discount rate: $10M × 1.02 ÷ 0.07 ≈ $146M.
terms.formula: TV = final cash flow × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)

terms.def: The blended return a company's lenders and shareholders expect. It is used as the discount rate in a DCF.
terms.example: A stable utility might use 6%; a young tech company 11%.

terms.def: What an analyst thinks a share is really worth based on its cash flows, as opposed to its market price.
terms.example: The DCF says $48 a share and the stock trades at $40: 20% upside.

terms.def: An analyst's call based on the gap between fair value and price. In Fin City, more than 15% upside is a Buy, more than 15% downside is a Sell, otherwise Hold.
terms.example: Fair value $60 and price $50 is 20% upside: a Buy.

cards.title: A company is its future cash
cards.body: A DCF forecasts free cash flow for a few years, adds a terminal value for everything after, and discounts it all at the WACC to get enterprise value. Subtract net debt for equity value and divide by shares for a value per share.

cards.title: A five-year DCF
cards.body: Free cash flow next year is $10M, growing 5% a year for 5 years; the WACC is 9% and growth after that is 2%. The five years are worth about $43M today. Terminal value ≈ $12.2M × 1.02 ÷ 0.07 ≈ $177M, worth about $115M today. Enterprise value ≈ $158M. Net debt $18M leaves $140M of equity; with 10M shares that's $14 a share.

cards.title: The steps
cards.body: PV of each year = cash flow ÷ (1 + WACC)^t. TV = last cash flow × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g). EV = sum of the PVs + PV of the TV. Value per share = (EV − net debt) ÷ shares. Upside = fair value ÷ price − 1.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Trusting a DCF's precision. Small changes in the growth rate or WACC swing the answer a lot, especially through the terminal value. Treat the result as a range.

checks.prompt: What happens to a DCF value if the WACC rises?
checks.explanation: Future cash is discounted more heavily, so it's worth less today.

checks.prompt: Fair value is $55 and the price is $50. What is the upside, and the Fin City rating?
checks.explanation: $55 ÷ $50 − 1 = 10%, below the 15% needed for a Buy, so Hold.

checks.prompt: Equity value is $300M and there are 20M shares. What is the value per share?

terms.def: What a startup is valued at just before new investment comes in.
terms.example: $8M pre-money, and it raises $2M.

terms.def: The pre-money value plus the new money raised. The investor's stake is their investment divided by the post-money.
terms.example: $8M + $2M = $10M post-money, so the investor owns 20%.
terms.formula: post-money = pre-money + investment; investor % = investment ÷ post-money

terms.def: When a company issues new shares, existing owners' percentages shrink, even if their shares become more valuable.
terms.example: A founder with 60% sells 20% of the company to an investor and now owns 48%.

terms.def: A table of who owns how many shares and what percent of the company.
terms.example: Founders 70%, seed investors 20%, employee option pool 10%.

terms.def: Investors with preferred shares are paid first when the company is sold. With a 1x non-participating preference they take the larger of their money back or their share as if converted.
terms.example: An investor put in $5M for 25%. The company sells for $12M: 25% would be $3M, so they take their $5M back and common shareholders split $7M.

terms.def: The right to buy company shares later at a fixed strike price. Valuable only if the share price ends up above the strike.
terms.example: Options with a $2 strike when shares are worth $10 are worth $8 each.

terms.def: The fixed price at which an option lets you buy the shares.
terms.example: Strike $5 and share price $12: each option is worth $7 if exercised.
terms.formula: option value at exercise = max(0, share price − strike)

terms.def: Earning your options or shares over time. A typical plan vests over 4 years with a 1-year cliff: nothing until the first anniversary, then 25%, then monthly.
terms.example: Leave after 10 months with a 1-year cliff and you keep none of the options.

cards.title: Selling slices of the future
cards.body: Startups raise money by selling new shares. The price is set by the pre-money valuation; new money plus pre-money gives the post-money. Each round dilutes earlier owners. When the company is sold, preferred investors are paid by their liquidation preferences before common shareholders and employees with options.

cards.title: Two rounds and a sale
cards.body: Founders own 100%. Seed: $2M at $8M pre-money, so post-money is $10M, the investor gets 20% and the founders 80%. Series A: $10M at $30M pre, post $40M, the new investor gets 25% and everyone else is scaled by 0.75: founders 60%, seed 15%. A sale for $200M gives the founders' 60% $120M.

cards.title: Round maths
cards.body: Post-money = pre-money + investment. New investor % = investment ÷ post-money. Everyone else's % after = old % × (1 − new investor %). Option payoff = max(0, price − strike) × vested options.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Thinking dilution always hurts. Owning 60% of a $40M company beats 100% of a $5M one. What matters is the value of your stake, not the percent.

checks.prompt: An investor puts $3M into a startup at a $9M pre-money valuation. What percent do they own?
You own 40% before a round that sells 20% of the company to a new investor. What is your new stake?
Options with a $4 strike when the shares are worth $3. What are they worth if exercised now?
checks.explanation: You'd pay $4 for a $3 share, so you wouldn't exercise: they're worth $0.
